Name: regularization_backfire_small_data
Title: When Regularization Backfires in Small-Data Image Classification
Short Hypothesis: Common regularization techniques are supposed to help when data is scarce, but sometimes they hurt. There are conditions under which standard regularization backfires in low-data image classification, and characterizing them is useful.
Related Work: Practitioners apply dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and label smoothing almost reflexively on small datasets, assuming they curb overfitting. Yet some regularizers interact badly with small-sample regimes, with each other, or with particular architectures, and can leave a model worse off than a plain baseline. This phenomenon is encountered often but rarely reported systematically.
Abstract: Practitioners reach for regularization almost reflexively when training on small datasets, on the assumption that these techniques curb overfitting and improve generalization. Yet in practice the picture is murkier: some regularizers interact badly with small-sample regimes, with each other, or with particular architectures, and can leave a model worse off than a plain baseline. This work explores the conditions under which standard regularization backfires in low-data image classification. We aim to characterize the failure modes, identify which combinations are most fragile, and surface practical guidance about when a regularizer is likely to help versus hurt.
Experiments: Investigate several common regularization techniques (such as dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and label smoothing) on small-data image classification.
Compare regularized models against an unregularized baseline and identify when regularization reduces performance.
Analyze which regularizers or combinations are most fragile in the low-data regime.
Summarize practical guidance on when a regularizer is likely to help versus hurt.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Findings may depend heavily on the specific dataset, architecture, and training budget chosen.
Without a pinned protocol, results may be hard to reproduce or compare across runs.
Compute constraints may limit the breadth of conditions that can be explored.
